author: Erich Maria Remarque
introFa: کتاب «Arch of Triumph» نوشته Erich Maria Remarque یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Arch of Triumph»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

What does 'Hellenistico-Roman' mean? It may be used to contrast with 'Hellenistic' (p. 77), or it may seemingly signify the whole Hellenistic and Roman periods (p. 122). One may also question the wisdom of including in the Index a heading 'Alexandria' which occupies three-quarters of the whole. The volume of plates is bedevilled by a lack of scales, although often measurements are given in the text, and some of the figures are not of the first quality (figs, no, 327). Nevertheless, the volumes remain very useful. But it was incautious of the author to vaunt his disdain of the close study of archaeological evidence (p. 36). Westfield College, London M. A. R. COLL EDGE ARCH OF TRIUMPH RICHARD BRILLIANT : The Arch of Septimius Severus in the Roman Forum. (Memoirs of the American Academy in Rome, xxix.) Pp. 271; 98 plates, 108 figs. Rome: American Academy in Rome, 1967. Cloth. THE triple Arch of Septimius Severus is one of the most complete and familiar of all the monuments of ancient Rome; yet it had to wait until 1967 to enjoy the honour of a full-dress, scientific publication. Two previous endeavours to provide this, both cut short by death, had been made by members of the American Academy in Rome, H. E. Askew (1932-3) and E. C. Olsen (1937-9), during the course of which many important observations and discoveries were made and much valuable photographic material was collected. Now the enterprise has been triumphantly carried through by Richard Brilliant, Fellow of the Academy from i960 to 1962, who, while using his predecessors' work, has undertaken a completely fresh and independent study of the monu- ment, both as a piece of architecture and as a storehouse of Severan sculpture, and has added numerous new photographs, diagrams, and plans. The Arch was erected, so its flamboyant inscription informs us, in 203 and is seen by Brilliant as essentially a calculated product of imperial propaganda, with the twofold aim of boosting Septimius' Parthian victories and of pro- claiming the legitimacy and 'millenaristic character' of the Severan dynasty. The present treatment of the monument falls into three main parts, of which the first part deals with its structure, architectural ornament, site, and inscrip- tion ; the second part covers the sculptured reliefs on its keystones and spandrels, in the narrow friezes above its lateral passageways, and on the pedestals supporting its decorative columns, four on each facade; while the third part is devoted to the Arch's most original feature, its four great panels of highly pictorial historical reliefs, two on each facade above the lateral passageways. Every structural and sculptural element is minutely described, catalogued, and stylistically analysed; and comparisons, as acute as they are detailed, are fruitfully drawn, not only between the Severan Arch in Rome and die earlier metropolitan Arches of Augustus, Titus, and Trajan and the contemporary Arch of the Severi at Lepcis Magna, but also, in the case of the great panels, between their historical scenes and those of the State reliefs of the second century and particularly those in the winding bands of the Trajanic and Aurelian Columns. THE CLASSICAL REVIEW 231 Antique; and to some extent this is obviously true. But as the present volume makes vividly clear, the designers and carvers of the sculpture of Septimius' Roman Arch, at any rate, were firmly rooted in the classical and Antonine tradition and deeply indebted for inspiration to their metropolitan models. In the great panels Brilliant does, indeed, seek to differentiate between an 'Antonine' and a 'Severan' master; but there, as elsewhere in the book, his stylistic distinctions tend to be a trifle over-subtle and do not always strike one as completely cogent. (A similar kind of criticism might be made of the section in Part i on the Arch's topography. Were the reasons for the choice of site really so refined ? Was there, in fact, any other Forum site still available ?) These four panels were, indeed, in themselves a novelty—the first appearance on a Roman arch of the narrative, documentary rendering of military events, as contrasted with ceremonial or symbolic scenes; and Brilliant's discussion of them is, perhaps, his most important contribution to our understanding and appreciation of the monument. Most satisfactory are his identifications of their military content—the surrender of Nisibis (SE.), the surrender of Edessa (NE.), the capture of Babylon and Seleucia (NW.), the capture of Ctesiphon (SW.), all to be 'read' in their true chronological sequence, as one passes round the Arch from the south end of the 'Forum' fagade, to the corresponding end of the 'Gapitoline'. Within each panel, as Brilliant demonstrates, the various incidents depicted, sieges, marches, fights, imperial adlocutiones, councils of war, submissions of Parthians, etc., must be 'read' from the bottom upwards; and in this sense there is a certain resemblance between the Severan method of narration and that of the Columns with their climbing ribbons of relief-work that starts at the base. But the genuine 'continuous' style is not to be found in the work of Septimius' designers. Not only does each panel form a self-contained and independent picture of a special episode of the Parthian War, but the incidents of which that episode is composed are, in their turn, carefully selected for a deliberate, propagandist purpose. What we have on the Arch is not a flowing epic, an unbroken chain of happenings, great and small, but a series of highlighted and always significant dramatic acts. The illustrations are of very fine quality and include, not only a complete documentation of the Arch itself, but also a most valuable assemblage of comparative material. Misprints are few and the over-all production is first- class. Brilliant's book can justly claim to be a notable addition to the Memoirs and to represent the definitive work on its subject—at least for a long time to come. Oxford J. M. C.
